title: What Medical Conditions Can Disqualify You From Medigap?

payload.title: What Medical Conditions Can Disqualify You From Medigap?
payload.excerpt: Medigap underwriting varies by insurer and state, with no single list of disqualifying conditions. Timing your application during protected windows matters more than any diagnosis.
payload.author: David Haass
payload.imageAlt: What Medical Conditions Can Disqualify You From Medigap?
payload.seoTitle: Medical Conditions That Disqualify You From Medigap
payload.seoDescription: Learn what medical conditions can disqualify you from Medigap and how timing your application correctly can affect underwriting decisions and approval

structuredSections.text: What Medical Conditions Can Disqualify You From Medigap? A Quick Answer

structuredSections.content: Outside your [[Medigap Open Enrollment Period](/faqs/medicare-supplement-open-enrollment/)](/faqs/medigap-open-enrollment/) or a guaranteed issue situation, insurers are generally allowed to use [medical underwriting](/faqs/medicare-supplement-plans-and-pre-existing-conditions/) to review your [health history](/faqs/medicare-coverage-for-disabled-under-65/) before deciding whether to approve your application and what to charge you. There is no single published federal list that names exact disqualifying diagnoses, because underwriting criteria vary by insurance company and by state. Conditions like serious heart disease, active cancer treatment, or kidney failure often draw closer scrutiny, but the outcome depends on the insurer you apply with.

The timing of your application usually matters more than any single health condition. If you apply during a protected window, your health history generally cannot be used against you. If you apply later and face a denial, you still have options to consider.

structuredSections.calloutText:
Timing your Medigap application, not any single diagnosis, is usually the biggest factor in whether underwriting affects you.
During your [Medigap Open Enrollment Period](/faqs/medicare-supplement-open-enrollment/) or a guaranteed issue event, insurers cannot use your health answers to deny you or raise your price.
Outside those windows, underwriting criteria differ by insurer, so a denial from one company does not mean denial everywhere.
If you are denied, compare other [Medigap insurers](/faqs/top-10-medicare-supplement-insurance-companies/), consider a [Medicare Advantage plan](/faqs/medicare-advantage-vs-medicare-supplement/), or speak with a [licensed agent](/faqs/medicare-and-employer-coverage/) before assuming you have no options left.

structuredSections.text: What Is Medical Underwriting, and When Do Medigap Insurers Use It?

structuredSections.content: Medical underwriting is the process an insurer uses to review your health history and decide whether to approve your Medigap application, and if so, at what premium. It typically involves a health questionnaire asking about current conditions, past diagnoses, hospitalizations, and medications you take.

During your [Medigap Open Enrollment Period](/faqs/medicare-supplement-open-enrollment/), or if you have a guaranteed issue right, insurers cannot use your answers to medical questions to deny you a policy or change your price based on your health history, according to [Medicare.gov guidance on buying a Medigap policy](https://www.medicare.gov/health-drug-plans/medigap/ready-to-buy/how). Outside those protections, underwriting typically applies in a few common situations:

items: You apply for Medigap after your initial six-month enrollment window has closed
You want to switch from one Medigap plan to another later on, without a qualifying event
You are applying for the first time without a guaranteed issue right in place

structuredSections.content: Because underwriting decisions are made by each insurance company individually, the same health history can lead to different results depending on who you apply with. One insurer might approve your application with a standard premium, while another might decline it or offer different terms, based on its own internal guidelines.

structuredSections.text: How the Underwriting Process Usually Works

structuredSections.content: While the exact process varies by company, most Medigap underwriting follows a similar general sequence.

items: You complete a health questionnaire as part of your application, answering questions about diagnoses, treatments, and medications
The insurer reviews your medical history, which may include requesting records from your doctor for more detail on certain conditions
The insurer issues a decision: full approval, approval with modified terms, or denial

structuredSections.text: How Do Health Conditions Affect Medigap Eligibility?

structuredSections.content: Insurers generally weigh [chronic illness](/faqs/medicare-coverage-for-mental-health/)es, recent hospitalizations, and ongoing treatment plans more heavily than conditions that are stable or resolved. A diagnosis by itself rarely tells the whole story. What matters more is how the condition is currently being managed and what kind of future costs it might signal to an insurer evaluating risk.

Having a health condition does not automatically mean you will be denied. Severity, how recently you were diagnosed, and whether your treatment is ongoing or completed all play a role in the decision. A chronic illness that is well controlled with stable treatment is often viewed differently than one involving frequent hospital visits or an unpredictable course of care.

If you are living with a chronic illness and wondering whether Medigap is still within reach, the honest answer is that it depends on the specifics of your case and the insurer you approach. Conditions that are newly diagnosed, actively being treated, or associated with frequent complications tend to make approval harder. Conditions that are long-stable, well managed, or in remission are often more manageable for underwriters to evaluate favorably.

structuredSections.text: What Disqualifies You From Medigap Coverage? Conditions That Commonly Raise Red Flags

structuredSections.content: Insurers generally focus on conditions associated with high or unpredictable future medical costs. There is no single universal list that applies across every company, since underwriting criteria differ by insurer. That said, certain categories of conditions tend to come up often enough that they are worth discussing directly with any insurer or licensed agent before you apply:

items: End-stage renal disease, given the ongoing and often costly treatment it requires
Certain active cancers, particularly those currently in treatment rather than in remission
Serious heart conditions, including those involving recent surgery, hospitalization, or unstable symptoms
Diabetes with complications, as opposed to diabetes that is well controlled without secondary issues

structuredSections.content: The presence of multiple conditions together, or a health history that involves frequent hospital care, can carry more weight in an underwriting decision than a single stable diagnosis on its own. Rather than assuming you will be disqualified based on one diagnosis, it is worth asking an insurer or a licensed agent directly how your specific health history might be evaluated. Underwriting outcomes are company-specific, so a condition that creates a problem with one insurer may not with another.}

Before you apply for Medigap outside a protected window, ask a licensed agent to help you compare how two or three different insurers in your area tend to handle your specific health conditions. A little research before you submit an application can save you from an unnecessary denial on your record.

structuredSections.text: When Can't Insurers Deny You? Understanding Guaranteed Issue Rights

structuredSections.content: Guaranteed issue rights, sometimes called Medigap protections, are specific situations outside your [Medigap Open Enrollment Period](/faqs/medicare-supplement-open-enrollment/) in which an insurer must sell you a Medigap policy regardless of your health conditions, as described in the [official Medicare guide to choosing a Medigap policy](https://www.medicare.gov/publications/02110-choosing-a-medigap-policy.pdf#page=17). These protections exist precisely because underwriting would otherwise apply, and they give certain beneficiaries a path to coverage without a health review.

Guaranteed issue rights are tied to particular life events and specific timeframes, which means acting quickly after a qualifying event matters. Missing the window tied to your situation could mean losing the protection and facing underwriting instead.

If you believe you may qualify for a guaranteed issue right, it helps to gather documentation of the triggering event, such as a notice from a previous plan or employer, before you apply. If you are unsure whether your situation qualifies, a licensed agent can review the details with you and help you understand your options without pressure.

structuredSections.text: Can a Medigap Insurer Charge Higher Premiums Instead of Denying You?

structuredSections.content: Underwriting outcomes are not always a simple approval or denial. In some cases, an insurer may offer coverage with different terms based on your health history, which is why it is worth asking each insurer directly how a specific condition might affect your offer rather than assuming a standard outcome.

Outside guaranteed issue protections, each insurer sets its own approach to pricing and underwriting conditions. This is one of the main reasons comparing multiple companies matters when you are applying outside a protected window; one insurer's response to your health history will not necessarily match another's.

Because this area varies so much by company, confirming the details directly with an insurer or a licensed agent is more reliable than assuming there is a standard industry practice you can count on in advance.

structuredSections.text: What Should You Do If You're Denied a Medigap Policy?

structuredSections.content: A denial from one insurer is not the end of the road. Several options are worth weighing before you decide on your next move.

items: Wait for your next [Medigap Open Enrollment Period](/faqs/medicare-supplement-open-enrollment/) or a future guaranteed issue event, if one may apply to your situation
Consider a [Medicare Advantage plan](/faqs/medicare-advantage-vs-medicare-supplement/) instead, since these plans generally do not use medical underwriting for approval
Ask about applying with a different Medigap insurer or a different plan letter, since underwriting standards vary by company
Work with a licensed agent to re-evaluate your situation and identify which paths are realistically available to you

structuredSections.content: [Medicare Advantage plan](/faqs/medicare-advantage-vs-medicare-supplement/)s are generally worth comparing if Medigap approval feels uncertain, since they typically do not require applicants to pass a health review during open enrollment periods. The coverage structure is different from Medigap, so it is worth understanding those differences rather than treating it as an automatic substitute.}

A denial can feel discouraging, especially if you were counting on a particular plan. It is a setback, not a dead end. Many people who are denied by one insurer still find coverage through another company, a different plan letter, or a future enrollment opportunity.

structuredSections.text: How State Rules Can Affect Your Underwriting Experience

structuredSections.content: Some states offer additional consumer protections or enrollment opportunities beyond the federal minimums that apply nationwide. These variations can affect how underwriting works where you live, including whether you have access to extra windows for applying without a health review.

Because rules can differ meaningfully depending on where you live, it is worth confirming your own state's specific protections with a licensed agent or your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) rather than relying on general information alone.

State variation is one more reason personalized guidance tends to be more reliable than a general article. What applies in one state may not apply in yours, and a licensed agent or SHIP counselor can confirm the rules that actually govern your application.

structuredSections.text: Planning Your Next Step With Confidence

structuredSections.content: Understanding how underwriting works, and how your own health history fits into that process, can help you avoid surprises when you apply for a Medigap policy. Timing your application around your [Medigap Open Enrollment Period](/faqs/medicare-supplement-open-enrollment/) or a guaranteed issue event remains the most reliable way to avoid a health review altogether.

If you are unsure how your specific conditions might be viewed by insurers, talking with a licensed Medicare agent can help you get clear, pressure-free answers before you apply. Getting personalized information now is a more solid foundation than guessing and risking a denial or an unexpected gap in coverage.

structuredSections.text: Frequently Asked Questions About Medigap and Health Conditions

faqs.question: What medical conditions make you ineligible for Medigap?
faqs.answer: Eligibility depends on each insurer's own underwriting criteria rather than one universal list. Conditions like serious heart disease, active cancer treatment, or kidney failure are commonly scrutinized, but outcomes vary by company. The only guaranteed way to avoid a health-based denial is applying during your Medigap Open Enrollment Period or a guaranteed issue event.

faqs.question: Can you get Medigap with a chronic illness?
faqs.answer: A chronic illness does not automatically disqualify you from Medigap. How stable the condition is, your treatment history, and the specific insurer's underwriting rules all factor into the decision. Well-managed, stable conditions are often viewed differently than ones involving frequent hospitalizations or recent changes in treatment.

faqs.question: I'd rather read more on my own before I talk to anyone, is that okay?
faqs.answer: Yes, taking time to learn the basics first is a reasonable approach. Understanding how underwriting works and what guaranteed issue rights cover can help you ask better questions later. Help from a licensed agent is available whenever you feel ready to discuss your specific situation.

faqs.question: Will reaching out for help mean I get a pushy sales call?
faqs.answer: Licensed agents can walk through underwriting questions and your options without pressure, focused specifically on your health history and coverage goals. You can ask general questions about how underwriting works without committing to an application. The goal is to help you understand your situation, not to push a particular plan.

faqs.question: How do I know which source to trust for underwriting information?
faqs.answer: Official Medicare resources and licensed agents are reliable starting points for understanding how underwriting works. Be cautious about relying on a single insurer's marketing materials alone, since those may emphasize their own products rather than giving you a full picture of your options across companies.

faqs.question: What if I apply and get denied? Will that follow me later?
faqs.answer: A denial from one insurer does not necessarily affect your eligibility with another, since each company sets its own underwriting standards. This is one reason comparing multiple insurers can help if your first application is turned down. A denial limits that specific offer, not your ability to apply elsewhere.

faqs.question: How do I qualify for Medigap without going through underwriting?
faqs.answer: The two main ways to avoid medical underwriting are applying during your Medigap Open Enrollment Period, which starts when you are 65 and enrolled in Part B, or applying during a guaranteed issue event tied to a qualifying life situation. Outside those windows, insurers can generally review your health history.

faqs.question: How can I avoid choosing a plan I later regret?
faqs.answer: Compare coverage, costs, and access to your doctors and prescriptions with a licensed agent before enrolling, rather than deciding based on the monthly premium alone. A lower premium can come with tradeoffs that matter more once you actually need care, so looking at the full picture helps prevent regret later.

keyTakeaways: No federal list of disqualifying conditions exists; underwriting criteria vary by insurer and state
During Medigap Open Enrollment or a guaranteed issue event, insurers cannot deny you or raise prices based on health history
Conditions like serious heart disease, active cancer treatment, or kidney failure often draw closer underwriting scrutiny
A denial from one insurer does not mean denial from all, since each company sets its own underwriting standards
If denied, you can compare other Medigap insurers, consider Medicare Advantage, or consult a licensed agent
